title: Cyber Defenders Unit 4 · Tricks and tricksters (6-8)

items.q: A message shows the sender name 'School Office', but the real address behind it belongs to a stranger. What is the costume here?
choices: The real address behind the name
The friendly sender name
The time the message arrived
The spelling in the subject line
items.why: Anyone can type a friendly name like School Office. The name is the costume; the real address shows who sent it.

items.q: A link's words say 'Library prize page', but the address behind the words leads somewhere else entirely. What should you trust?
choices: The words written on the link
Its bright, official-looking colors
The real address the link leads to
How many people shared it
items.why: Link words and colors can say anything. Only the real address behind them shows where the link goes.

items.q: A message you did not expect arrives with a file attached and asks you to open it fast. What is the verify-first response?
choices: Open it quickly before it expires
Reply and ask the sender for more files
Forward it to friends so they can check it
Do not open it; check with the real sender another way and tell a trusted adult
items.why: An unexpected file with a rush is a classic trap. Do not open it; check with the real sender another way.

items.q: A trickster sends fake prize messages hoping people will hand over money. Which threat actor is this?
choices: The spy, who wants secrets
The vandal, who wants damage
The scammer, who wants money
The account thief, who wants in
items.why: Fake prizes that end with a payment want money. That is the scammer, not the spy, the vandal or the account thief.

items.q: Two people test a school network's locks. One has clear permission and the other does not. What makes one of them ethical?
choices: Working at night
Having permission
Using faster tools
Knowing more secrets
items.why: Ethical testing is about permission. Tools, timing and know-how are the same for both people; only one was allowed.

items.q: An account thief keeps trying to get into students' accounts. Which defense fits this actor best?
choices: Strong, separate passphrases and a second proof step
Sharing posts as widely as possible
Opening every attachment to check it
Turning off every lock to save time
items.why: An account thief wants to get in. Strong, separate passphrases and a second proof step are the locks made for that.

items.q: A post claims a famous singer is giving away prizes, but only if you tap its link and share it within ten minutes. What kind of false is this?
choices: A hoax that wants your belief
Rage-bait that wants your reaction
A scam that wants your tap
A fine, ordinary post
items.why: It wants a tap on its link within ten minutes: a scam. A hoax wants belief, and rage-bait wants your reaction.

items.q: A shocking claim about your school is spreading fast. What is the first check?
choices: Share it before it disappears
Find another trusted source saying the same thing
Judge it by how real the picture looks
Count how many friends have shared it
items.why: Speed, a realistic picture and many shares prove nothing. A second trusted source saying the same thing is the first check.

items.q: Why is sharing a fake post the payload the trickster is counting on?
choices: Sharing deletes the fake for everyone
Sharing proves the post must be true
Sharing makes the picture clearer
Sharing carries the fake to everyone who trusts you
items.why: A fake spreads through people who trust each other. Each share carries it further, which is exactly what the trickster wants.
